palpate

PAL-payt — stress on first syllable, rhymes with allocate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To palpate something is to examine a part of the body by pressing on it with the hands, in the deliberate, diagnostic way a doctor checks a patient's condition.

The doctor palpated the swollen ankle to check for a break.

Example

The doctor palpated Maria's abdomen, pressing gently with her fingers to feel for any lumps or tender spots; the careful exam revealed that her appendix was inflamed.

Palpate is the precise word for medical examination by touch. A plain word like 'pressed' or 'felt' would miss the specific, clinical intent—palpate means to examine by hand in a deliberate, diagnostic way.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

probe: To probe is to explore something carefully in search of what is hidden, often with an instrument — a dentist probes a cavity, a robot probes the seafloor. To palpate is narrower: hands only, pressing a part of the body to judge its condition.

examine: To examine is to check something closely and carefully, by any method at all — eyes, questions, scans, or tests. To palpate names one exact method of examining: pressing with the hands, the deliberate way a doctor checks the body by touch.

manipulate: To manipulate is to handle or work something skillfully with the hands — a therapist manipulates a stiff joint to loosen it, shaping and adjusting it. To palpate is not about changing anything: the hands press only to learn what the tissue underneath is like.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ignore: to give something no attention whatsoever

overlook: to miss or fail to check something

Where it sits · how thorough and invasive the exam

touch → press → palpate → dissect

touch vs. palpate: To touch is far weaker than to palpate — touching is brief, casual contact, while palpating is deliberate, careful pressing to learn about what is underneath.

press vs. palpate: To press is weaker than to palpate; pressing is just applying force, while palpating is pressing skillfully and with a purpose: to examine.

dissect vs. palpate: To dissect is stronger than to palpate — palpating examines something from the outside with the hands, while dissecting cuts it open to examine every part inside.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — palp: to touch gently, stroke (Latin)

Suffix — -ate: to act on, to do (Latin)

Put it together: The root palp- ('to touch gently') + -ate (a verb-forming suffix, 'to act on') literally means 'to act by touching' — to palpate is to examine something with careful, probing touch.

Use the root in a new word: palpable: The tension in the room was palpable — so thick you could almost touch it — because palpable and palpate both come from the Latin palpare, 'to touch.'

formal / medical
